title: Nouns, Number, and Class
summary: The plural in -లు, and the division of nouns that Telugu makes where European languages make gender — a division that draws its line in one place in the singular and in quite another in the plural.

rules.heading: The Plural in -లు
rules.statement: The plural of a Telugu noun is made by adding **-లు** to it. There is one plural ending and not several, which is a considerable simplification after a language of declensions; the difficulty lies not in the ending but in what the stem does before it.

examples.note: abbāyi → abbāyilu; the stem is untouched

rules.heading: What the Stem Does Before -లు
rules.statement: Many nouns change before the plural ending, and the changes fall into a few regular kinds. A noun in **-ం** replaces it with a long vowel; a noun in **-లు** or **-డు** turns that consonant into **-ళ్ళు**. These are not exceptions to be memorised singly but classes to be recognised.

paradigms.caption: Stem changes before -లు

cells: the anusvāra gives way to a long vowel

rows.label: -లు → -ళ్ళు
cells: l becomes a doubled retroflex ḷ

rows.label: -డు → -డ్లు
cells: the ḍ is kept and l added beneath it

rows.label: -ి → -ులు
cells: a vowel comes in before the ending

paradigms.footnote: The commonest of all is the first: nouns in -ం, which are very numerous, all make their plural in -ాలు.

rules.heading: Mahat and Amahat
rules.statement: Telugu divides its nouns not by gender but by **class**: **మహత్** (mahat), the *high* class, and **అమహత్** (amahat), the rest. The division is not made in the same place in both numbers, and that is the single most surprising thing about Telugu grammar. It is not a quirk of the pronouns only: the verb agrees with the same division (¶55), so a learner who gets the class wrong gets the verb wrong too.

rules.heading: The Singular: Men against Everything Else
rules.statement: In the **singular**, the mahat class contains **male human beings and nothing else**. A woman, an animal and a stone belong together in the amahat class, and take the same pronoun **అది** and the same verb form. This strikes a European ear as strange, and it is best learned as a fact about the grammar rather than argued with.

paradigms.caption: The singular division

rows.label: అమహత్
cells: a woman, an animal, a thing

paradigms.footnote: **ఆమె** is also used of a woman, and is the polite and usual word in modern speech; but the *grammar* — the verb ending — treats her as amahat all the same.

examples.gloss: she — amahat by grammar, whichever word is used

rules.heading: The Plural: People against Things
rules.statement: In the **plural** the line moves. The mahat class now contains **all human beings, men and women alike**, and the amahat class only what is not human. A woman who was grouped with the stone in the singular is grouped with the man in the plural. Telugu is therefore a language in which the sexes are distinguished when they are alone and not when they are together.

examples.gloss: The girls are here. They are my friends.
examples.note: girls are human, so mahat — వాళ్ళు, never అవి

examples.gloss: The dogs are there. They are big.
examples.note: dogs are not human, so amahat — అవి

examples.target: ఆమె నా అమ్మ. అమ్మాయిలు నా స్నేహితులు — వాళ్ళు.
examples.roman: āme nā amma. ammāyilu nā snēhitulu — vāḷḷu.
examples.gloss: She is my mother. The girls are my friends — they.
examples.note: one woman is amahat; women together are mahat — the line has moved

examples.target: అబ్బాయిలు, అమ్మాయిలు ఇక్కడ — వాళ్ళు. పుస్తకాలు, చెట్లు అక్కడ — అవి.
examples.roman: abbāyilu, ammāyilu ikkaḍa — vāḷḷu. pustakālu, ceṭlu akkaḍa — avi.
examples.gloss: Boys and girls are here — they (people). Books and trees are there — they (things).
examples.note: both sexes share one plural pronoun; only the non-human takes అవి

rules.heading: The Personal Pronouns
rules.statement: The pronouns are given below. Note the first person plural, where Telugu makes a distinction English has not got: **మేము** excludes the person spoken to, **మనం** includes them. *We are here* is a different word according to whether you are including your hearer or speaking of yourself and others without them.

paradigms.caption: The personal pronouns
paradigms.footnote: **మీరు** is the polite singular as well as the plural, exactly as *jūs* is in Lithuanian and *vous* in French.

examples.gloss: I am Ravi. You are my elder brother.
examples.note: నువ్వు is the familiar singular — a friend, a child, an intimate

examples.gloss: We are here. You are there.
examples.note: మేము excludes the hearer; the second sentence is what shows the exclusion
మీరు to one person, politely — as well as to many

examples.target: ఆమె నా అమ్మ. అతను నా అన్న. వాళ్ళు నా స్నేహితులు. అవి నా పుస్తకాలు.
examples.roman: āme nā amma. atanu nā anna. vāḷḷu nā snēhitulu. avi nā pustakālu.
examples.gloss: She is my mother. He is my elder brother. They are my friends. They are my books.
examples.note: third person: class and number choose the pronoun — ఆమె / అతను / వాళ్ళు / అవి

vocabulary.gloss: the class of all other nouns

drills.explanation: -లు is added and the stem is untouched. This is the simplest of the plural classes.
A noun in -ం gives up its anusvāra for a long vowel before -లు: *pustakaṃ → pustakālu*. Nouns of this shape are very numerous, so the class is worth knowing first.

drills.stem: In the **singular**, which of these belongs to the మహత్ class?
drills.explanation: In the singular the mahat class holds male human beings and nothing else. A woman is grammatically amahat, grouped with the dog and the book — the fact a European learner finds hardest to accept.

drills.stem: **అమ్మాయిలు ఇక్కడ. ___ నా స్నేహితులు.** Which pronoun fills the blank?
drills.explanation: Girls are human, and in the plural every human being is mahat — so *వాళ్ళు*, not *అవి*. *అది* and *ఆమె* are singular.

drills.stem: Which of these are correct plurals?
drills.explanation: The last is wrong: a noun in -ం gives up the anusvāra, making *పుస్తకాలు*. The other three show three different stem-classes, all regular.

drills.stem: You are speaking to a friend and mean *we* — yourself and that friend. Which sentence is right?
drills.explanation: *మనం ఇక్కడ* includes the hearer. *మేము ఇక్కడ* would mean you and others, but not the person you are talking to.

drills.stem: **మీరు ఎవరు?** — said to one stranger. Why *మీరు* and not *నువ్వు*?
options: Because *మీరు* is the polite singular as well as the plural.
Because *నువ్వు* is only used of women.
drills.explanation: *మీరు* serves as both the plural and the polite singular, as *jūs* does in Lithuanian. *నువ్వు* is for a friend, a child, or an intimate.

drills.stem: Which statements about the Telugu class system are correct?
options: In the singular, a woman is grammatically amahat.
In the plural, a woman is grammatically mahat.
The class system divides nouns the same way in both numbers.
The verb agrees with the class, not merely the pronoun.
drills.explanation: The line is drawn in one place in the singular and another in the plural — that is the whole peculiarity. And it is not confined to the pronouns: the verb ending follows the same division (¶55).

drills.stem: **ఆమె** is the ordinary polite word for *she*. What does that change about her grammatical class?
options: It makes her mahat in the singular.
Nothing: the verb still treats her as amahat.
It makes her mahat in the plural only.
It removes her from the class system.
drills.explanation: The word chosen and the grammatical class are two different things. Whichever pronoun is used, the singular verb ending for a woman is the amahat one — which is why the class must be learned as grammar and not as vocabulary.

drills.stem: Of **a man, a woman, a dog, and a book**, how many are మహత్ in the **singular**?
drills.explanation: One — the man. In the singular the mahat class holds male human beings only. Answering two counts the woman, which is exactly the assumption a European learner brings and must give up.

drills.stem: Of **men, women, dogs, and books**, how many are మహత్ in the **plural**?
drills.explanation: Two — men and women, who are together mahat once they are plural. Compare the previous question: the same four kinds of thing, and a different answer, because the line moves between the numbers.

drills.stem: **కుక్కలు అక్కడ. ___ పెద్దవి.** Which pronoun fills the blank?
drills.explanation: Dogs are not human, so in the plural they remain amahat — *అవి*. *వాళ్ళు* is only for people.

drills.stem: You and your friends are here; the person you are talking to is somewhere else. Which sentence fits?
drills.explanation: *మేము* excludes the hearer; *మీరు అక్కడ* makes the exclusion plain. *మనం ఇక్కడ* would pull the hearer into the group.

drills.stem: Which of these sentences choose the **right** third-person pronoun?
drills.explanation: The second is wrong: dogs take *అవి*, not *వాళ్ళు*. Girls take *వాళ్ళు*; books take *అవి*; one woman takes *ఆమె* (or *అది*) — each by class and number.

drills.stem: Compare **ఆమె నా అమ్మ** with **అమ్మాయిలు నా స్నేహితులు — వాళ్ళు**. What has moved?
options: Nothing: a woman is amahat in both numbers.
The line of class: one woman is amahat, women together are mahat.
The pronoun is optional in the plural.
drills.explanation: That is the whole surprise of ¶42: the sexes are distinguished when alone and not when together. The same person who is *ఆమె* in the singular is one of *వాళ్ళు* in the plural.

drills.stem: **నేను రవి. నువ్వు నా అన్న.** What does **నువ్వు** mark about the relationship?
options: Familiar address — a friend, a child, an intimate.
drills.explanation: *నువ్వు* is the familiar singular. To a stranger one would ask *మీరు ఎవరు?*

drills.stem: In **ఆమె నా అమ్మ. అతను నా అన్న. వాళ్ళు నా స్నేహితులు. అవి నా పుస్తకాలు.** how many **different** third-person pronouns appear?
drills.explanation: Four: *ఆమె*, *అతను*, *వాళ్ళు*, *అవి* — singular woman, singular man, plural people, plural things. Telugu will not let one *they* cover the last two.

drills.title: ఇక్కడ ఎవరు?
drills.passage: ఇక్కడ అబ్బాయిలు, అమ్మాయిలు. వాళ్ళు నా స్నేహితులు. అక్కడ కుక్కలు, చెట్లు. అవి పెద్దవి. ఇది నా ఇల్లు. అక్కడ రెండు ఇళ్ళు. ఆమె నా అమ్మ. అతను నా అన్న.
drills.romanization: ikkaḍa abbāyilu, ammāyilu. vāḷḷu nā snēhitulu. akkaḍa kukkalu, ceṭlu. avi peddavi. idi nā illu. akkaḍa reṇḍu iḷḷu. āme nā amma. atanu nā anna.
drills.translation: Here are boys and girls. They are my friends. There are dogs and trees. They are big. This is my house. There are two houses. She is my mother. He is my elder brother.

glossary.పెద్దవి: big (the plural form of పెద్ద used as a predicate)

questions.stem: Which pronoun does the passage use of the boys and girls together?
questions.explanation: *వాళ్ళు నా స్నేహితులు.* Boys and girls together are human, and so mahat in the plural — one pronoun serves both sexes.

questions.stem: Which words in the passage are **plural**?
questions.explanation: *అబ్బాయిలు* and *కుక్కలు* add -లు plainly; *ఇళ్ళు* is the plural of ఇల్లు with its stem changed. *ఇల్లు* itself, in *ఇది నా ఇల్లు*, is singular — and it is the one that looks plural, ending in -లు already.

questions.stem: The passage refers to four groups: the children, the dogs, the trees, and the two houses. How many of the four are **అమహత్**?
questions.explanation: Three: dogs, trees and houses. Only the boys and girls are human, and so mahat. Had the passage spoken of one girl instead, she would have been amahat too — the class of a woman depends on the number she is in.
